q: 1. Which of the following is a relatively ductile material?
explain: Mild steel shows large plastic elongation before fracture, making it relatively ductile compared to the brittle options listed.

q: 2. The property of material by which it can be beaten or rolled into plates, is called
explain: Malleability is the ability to be hammered/rolled into thin sheets.

q: 3. A member which is subjected to reversible tensile or compressible stress may fail at a stress lower than the ultimate stress of the material. The property of metal, is called
explain: Failure under repeated/reversed stress below the ultimate stress is the fatigue phenomenon.

q: 4. The safe value of stress below which the material will not fail when subjected to reversal of stress is known as
explain: The endurance limit is the stress amplitude below which a material can withstand infinite stress reversals.

q: 5. The method of increasing fatigue resistance by over stressing the metal by successively increasing the loading is known as
explain: Coaxing improves fatigue strength by applying gradually increasing sub-critical stress cycles.

q: 6. The phenomenon of slow growth of strain under a steady tensile stress, i.e. increasing with time, is called
explain: Creep is time-dependent strain growth under sustained stress.

q: 7. If the value of Young's Modulus of elasticity for a material is zero, it implies that the material is
explain: Zero stiffness against elastic deformation implies the material deforms permanently/plastically under any stress.

q: 8. Limit of proportionality depends upon
explain: The proportional limit is a material property, varying with the type of material.

q: 9. The S.I. unit of modulus of elasticity is
explain: Modulus of elasticity has units of stress (force/area); the SI unit is N/m² (Pascal).

q: 10. Which of the following is dimensionless?
explain: Strain is a ratio of length change to original length — dimensionless.

q: 11. The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: At the yield point, strain increases disproportionately for a small increase in load.

q: 12. Which of the following gives Modulus of Elasticity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Young's Modulus (E) = linear stress / linear strain.

q: 13. The Young's Modulus of elasticity is defined as a ratio of stress & strain within the
explain: Hooke's Law (and hence E) is valid only within the elastic limit.

q: 14. Which of the following gives Modulus of Rigidity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (N/G) = shear stress / shear strain.

q: 15. Which of the following gives Bulk Modulus?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
ratio of the normal stress of equal magnitude on all six faces on a solid cube to the volumetric strain
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) = uniform normal stress / volumetric strain.

q: 16. Identify the correct relationship that exists among the modulus of elasticity (E), modulus of rigidity (N) and bulk modulus (k)
explain: Standard elastic-constants relation: E = 9KN / (3K + N).

q: 17. Normal strain is defined as
options: strain that is normal to shear strain
explain: Normal (linear) strain = change in length / original length.

q: 18. Shear strain is defined as
options: change in angle between planes at right angles
change in angles between two angles
explain: Shear strain is the change in the right angle between two originally perpendicular planes/lines.

q: 19. The modular ratio of two materials is defined as (E1 and E2 are the modulus of elasticity of the respective materials)
explain: Modular ratio m = E1/E2, used in composite-section analysis (e.g. RCC transformed sections).

q: 20. How does Young's Modulus vary with increase in temperature?
explain: Interatomic bonding weakens with rising temperature, reducing stiffness (E) for most materials.

q: 21. Which of the following materials will have the highest Young's Modulus?
explain: Among these, mild steel has the highest stiffness (E ≈ 200 GPa).

q: 22. What is strain energy?
options: energy that is spent for straining a body
energy stored in a body because of being strained
explain: Strain energy is the elastic energy stored within a body as a result of deformation.

q: 23. The strain energy stored by a member when strained within elastic limit, is known as
explain: Resilience is the strain energy stored (and recoverable) within the elastic range.

q: 24. Proof resilience is the greatest stored energy at
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a material can absorb without permanent deformation, i.e. up to the elastic limit.

q: 25. The stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the resistance offered by the material per unit area to a force
explain: Stress is the internal resisting force per unit area developed in response to an applied load.

q: 26. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
explain: Thermal stress only develops if expansion/contraction is restrained — hence it depends on the end/support conditions, not on cross-section or length directly.

q: 27. The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than necessary to continue it
less than necessary to continue it
more than necessary to stop it
less than necessary to continue it
explain: The upper yield point stress needed to start yielding is higher than the (lower) stress needed to continue/sustain plastic flow.

q: 28. The ratio of intensity of stress in a case of a suddenly applied load to that of a gradually applied load is
explain: A suddenly applied load produces twice the stress/deflection of the same load applied gradually.

q: 29. The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: This describes the yield point, where strain grows disproportionately fast relative to load.

q: 30. When equal and opposite forces applied to a body tend to elongate it, the stress produced is called
explain: Forces that pull a body apart (elongating it) produce tensile stress.

q: 31. The bending moment acting on the plane of an element will cause the following type of stress on the plane
explain: Bending moment produces normal (bending) stress that varies linearly across the section — tension on one side, compression on the other.

q: 32. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
options: decreases in proportion to the stress
increases in proportion to the stress
explain: As per the answer key for this set; near the elastic limit the linear stress–strain proportionality begins to break down.

q: 33. The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length is
explain: A conical bar under self-weight elongates only 1/3 as much as a prismatic bar of the same length and weight, due to the tapering cross-section.

q: 34. The ratio of change in volume to the original volume is called:
explain: Volumetric strain = change in volume / original volume, by definition.

q: 35. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely the maximum compressive stress is developed on the:
explain: For a typical sagging beam, the top fiber experiences maximum compressive stress.

q: 36. Fatigue is the failure of a material under:
options: constant loads but occasionally well above static load
varying loads well below ultimate static load
constant loads well below ultimate static load
varying loads well above ultimate static load
explain: Fatigue failure occurs from repeated/varying stress cycles, even when each individual cycle's stress is well below the material's ultimate static strength.

q: 37. If a rod is simultaneously pulled at both of its ends, it will be a case of:
explain: Equal and opposite pulling forces along the rod's axis constitute axial (tensile) loading.

q: 38. A member which does not regain its original shape after the load producing deformation is removed, is said to be:
explain: Irrecoverable deformation after unloading is the defining characteristic of plastic behavior.

q: 39. The law which states that within elastic limits strain produced is proportional to stress producing it is known as:
explain: This is the direct statement of Hooke's Law.

q: 40. Tensile internal force tends to:
explain: Tensile force pulls the member apart, causing elongation.

q: 41. Stress may be defined as force per unit:
explain: Stress = Force / Area, by definition.

q: 42. The unit failure stress is taken as:
explain: For design purposes, the ultimate stress is conventionally used as the reference 'failure' stress of the material.

q: 43. The velocity of a moving body is:
explain: Velocity has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector quantity.

q: 44. The forces which meet at one point but their lines of action do not lie in a plane, are called:
explain: Forces meeting at a single point (concurrent) but spread across different planes (non-coplanar) are non-coplanar concurrent forces.

q: 45. The tension in a cable supporting a lift:
options: is more when the lift is moving downwards
is less when the lift is moving upwards
Remains constant whether it moves downwards or upwards
is less when the lift is moving downwards
explain: When a lift accelerates downward, the net upward tension required is less than the static weight (T = m(g − a)).

q: 46. The centre of gravity of a triangle is at the point where three
options: perpendicular bisectors of the sides of the triangle meet
bisectors of the angle of the triangle meet
explain: The centroid of a triangle is the point where its three medians intersect.

q: 47. The total time of collision and restitution of two bodies, is called
explain: The combined duration of the compression and restitution phases of a collision is called the period of impact.

q: 48. Young's modulus is the ratio of
explain: Young's Modulus E = longitudinal (axial) stress / longitudinal strain.

q: 49. Mathematically, strain may be defined as
explain: Linear strain = change in length / original length, i.e. deformation per unit length.
